articles.title: ISSB Targets Location and Indigenous Communities in Nature Disclosure Plan
articles.summary:
The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) has proposed detailed nature-related disclosures for companies applying IFRS S1. Feedback is open until 19 February 2027, while the proposals do not yet have […]
The post ISSB Targets Location and Indigenous Communities in Nature Disclosure Plan appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ISSB Targets Location and Indigenous Communities in Nature Disclosure Plan
- Consultation deadline: The ISSB is seeking feedback on its proposals until 19 February 2027.
- Disclosure focus: Companies would explain how nature dependencies and impacts create material risks and opportunities.
- Flexible format: The ISSB is consulting on whether to issue a voluntary Practice Statement or another form of guidance.
The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) has proposed detailed nature-related disclosures for companies applying IFRS S1. Feedback is open until 19 February 2027, while the proposals do not yet have an effective date.
The proposals address material information about nature-related risks and opportunities that could affect a company’s prospects. They also cover how dependencies and impacts on nature create those risks and opportunities. The ISSB wants reporting to connect nature with climate, other sustainability matters and financial statement information.
“Whether it is access to water for production, to rivers for transportation or to bees for pollination, companies around the world depend on nature. When a company’s access to these environmental resources is threatened, the company can face risks and opportunities that affect its prospects. We believe companies that comply with an IFRS Sustainability Practice Statement on nature-related disclosures will be best placed to provide high-quality reporting to their investors,” said Emmanuel Faber, ISSB Chair.
RELATED ARTICLE: ISSB Moves Nature Reporting Toward TNFD Alignment
The ISSB drew extensively on the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) when preparing the proposals. In particular, they emphasise location and interactions with Indigenous Peoples, Local Communities and affected stakeholders. The ISSB also considered efficient use alongside Global Reporting Initiative Standards and European Sustainability Reporting Standards. “We recognise that companies are deeply engaged with applying IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 for the first time. What we’re proposing is to balance the need to give markets time to implement the ISSB Standards well, with the demand from investors for information on nature,” said Sue Lloyd, ISSB Vice-Chair.
The proposed Practice Statement would be a stand-alone part of the IFRS Foundation’s materials and undergo its full due process. Its content and drafting would not differ from a Standard. However, companies could claim compliance with ISSB Standards without following the Practice Statement. The proposals do not set an effective date, enforcement mechanism or company-size threshold.
Who It Affects
- Reporting companies: Companies could use the proposals to disclose material nature dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities.
- Investors: Investors would receive connected information spanning nature, climate, other sustainability risks and financial statements.
- Affected stakeholders: Disclosures would emphasise location and interactions with Indigenous Peoples, Local Communities and other affected groups.
- Implementing jurisdictions: Authorities can comment on whether the content should become a Practice Statement, a Standard or another form.
The Stakeholders at a Glance

articles.title: South Pole Finds 12% of Companies Equipped to Turn Climate Action Into Business Value
articles.summary:
South Pole’s 2026 Net Zero Report found that only 12% of surveyed companies had four foundations needed to deliver value from climate action. The climate solutions company surveyed 600 senior […]
The post South Pole Finds 12% of Companies Equipped to Turn Climate Action Into Business Value appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
South Pole Finds 12% of Companies Equipped to Turn Climate Action Into Business Value
- Action versus strategy: Although 90% report active climate initiatives, only 43% have an approved strategy under implementation.
- Funding bottleneck: Just 23% report approval for at least 75% of climate business cases submitted during the past 24 months.
- Stronger outcomes: The 12% meeting four execution criteria were nearly twice as likely to report several business benefits.
South Pole’s 2026 Net Zero Report found that only 12% of surveyed companies had four foundations needed to deliver value from climate action. The climate solutions company surveyed 600 senior business decision-makers across Europe and the United States.
The Value Delivery Gap
South Pole classified 12% of respondents as Advanced because they met all four criteria. These covered an implemented strategy, value creation and risk protection, climate-risk integration, and dedicated transition funding. The remaining 88% formed the Aspiring group. South Pole did not disclose survey field dates or a sector breakdown in the announcement.
The report calls the divide between climate activity and measurable results the “value delivery gap.” Although 77% include risk protection and value creation in their climate plans, 53% still describe their work as compliance-focused. Also, 95% reported barriers to capturing value from climate action. Siloed responsibility led the obstacles at 24%, while 20% cited different value measures across sustainability and finance teams.
Stronger Business Outcomes
Advanced companies were 91% more likely to report better operational efficiency or lower costs. They were also 91% more likely to report improved access to finance or financing terms. The group was 77% more likely to report winning customers, contracts or tenders, and 76% more likely to enter new markets.
“Although companies have climate initiatives underway, they are struggling to deliver value, such as turning that activity into funded, delivered decarbonisation and business value across their operations and value chain. Companies that have our foundational building blocks in place are approximately twice as likely to report business benefits such as reduced costs, improved operating efficiency, and improved access to finance. However, this is only around 1 in 10 companies. It’s time for leaders to establish these building blocks and operationalise our four suggested actions in order to close this value delivery gap,” said Dara Olufon, Global Head of Advisory at South Pole.
South Pole recommends prioritising interventions by emissions impact, economics, feasibility, risk, and business value. Companies should then assign executive ownership, secure dedicated budgets and CFO approval, and mobilise delivery across business functions. The fourth action requires emissions and value measurement from the start, supported by accounting, monitoring and reporting.
RELATED ARTICLE: South Pole Welcomes Sustainability Veteran Dr. Daniel Klier as New CEO
Who It Affects
- Corporate leaders: South Pole recommends assigning executive ownership and dedicated budgets to approved, executable climate plans.
- Finance teams: Climate business cases require consistent value measures and CFO or investment committee approval.
- Delivery functions: Sustainability, procurement, operations and supply-chain teams must coordinate implementation instead of working in silos.

articles.title: China to Add Petrochemicals to National Carbon Market - Briefs Finance
articles.summary: China to Add Petrochemicals to National Carbon Market  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
What changed
Beijing intends to add chemicals and petrochemicals next year to its cap and trade program, widening coverage to industries tied to oil processing. The market, which began in 2021, already includes power, cement, steel and aluminum.
During a Wednesday briefing held before COP31 convenes in Turkey next month, Li Gao - who serves as the country's top climate negotiator - spelled out the schedule. Adding these industries would move the system closer to covering 80% of total emissions under the scheme.
Why officials are doing this
The carbon market currently applies to 65% of emissions, equal to 8.3 billion tons a year. As the world's largest emitter, China targets about a 3% decline, over the five years through 2030, in the carbon intensity per unit of output within the market's scope.
Officials also see industrial pressures. The country's bloated refining sector, which makes fuels and chemicals, is under strain as oil demand eases with rapid electrification. Putting a price on carbon will probably speed the phaseout of some excess or outdated capacity.
When policy changes reshape industries, staying informed matters; sign up for the free Market Briefs newsletter to get concise daily context
How the policy will support cleaner tech
Draft rules released earlier this month say the environment ministry will offer carbon credits to help hard to abate sectors adopt cleaner technologies. The list includes green ammonia, batteries and biofuels.
What it means for investors
In plain English: coverage is set to broaden, and carbon costs could nudge older, surplus capacity out faster in oil linked industries. Investors may also watch areas named in the draft rules, since credits are slated to support adoption of green ammonia, batteries and biofuels. The bottom line: policy is moving toward wider coverage and modest intensity cuts through 2030, with attention on oil processing and uptake of specific clean technologies.

articles.title: WBCSD Finds Only 33% of Companies Say Targets Are on Track
articles.summary:
The World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD) found established sustainability reporting practices but uneven decision-useful evidence. Its Reporting Matters 2026 assessment reviewed public information from 194 member companies across […]
The post WBCSD Finds Only 33% of Companies Say Targets Are on Track appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
WBCSD Finds Only 33% of Companies Say Targets Are on Track
- Strategy coverage: WBCSD found more than 90% of assessed companies report a company-specific sustainability strategy.
- Progress gap: Although 97% have targets, only 33% clearly state whether those targets are on track.
- Financial link: Just 16% show evidence that different transition levers receive financial assessment.
The World Business Council for Sustainable Development (WBCSD) found established sustainability reporting practices but uneven decision-useful evidence. Its Reporting Matters 2026 assessment reviewed public information from 194 member companies across the Americas, Asia-Pacific and Europe, the Middle East and Africa. The findings focus on information available to boards, investors and other stakeholders.
More than 90% of companies report a company-specific sustainability strategy, typically informed by materiality and aligned with corporate strategy. Although 92% use a materiality assessment, only 49% clearly explain its integration into enterprise risk management. WBCSD did not specify the review period or the number of companies joining its strategic discussions. “Stakeholder expectations have evolved significantly over the last decade, and our reporting has evolved with them. Stakeholders want confidence that sustainability is embedded in governance and decision-making, not just reflected in the final report,” said Prabodha Acharya, Chief Sustainability Officer at JSW Group.
Quick anonymous worklife pollWhat's my daily work emissions burn, or savings?Powered by ESG News
WBCSD found that 60% disclose a transition plan covering actions, governance, incentives and progress reporting. However, only 16% show evidence of financially assessing different transition levers. Meanwhile, 97% have targets linked to material sustainability issues, but only 33% clearly report whether targets are on track. “Reporting matters when it drives better decisions. Companies have built strong foundations and reporting has matured considerably, but its true value lies in providing decision-useful insights that protect and strengthen positive business outcomes. What matters is whether companies produce information that helps investors, boards and other stakeholders understand strategic priorities, progress, and where further action is needed. The next step is making sure that information shapes decisions at the board table,” said Uta Jungermann, Director Reporting Matters and Membership Criteria at WBCSD.
Fewer than half of assessed companies, or 45%, transparently explain poor performance and corrective action. The assessment combines a systematic review with strategic discussions about what makes reporting useful in practice. WBCSD said the report starts a series examining how sustainability information is created, used and acted upon. “A reframe is exactly what’s required after what may well be the most challenging year yet for sustainability reporting. With the milestone of 2030 now looming, the opportunity to reframe for decision-useful, audience-first reporting that distinguishes for company robustness, and differentiation is precisely what Reporting Matters serves,” said Jennifer Crowley, Client Partner – Sustainability at Radley Yeldar.
Who It Affects
- Boards: The findings point to limited visibility on risk integration, financial assessment and corrective action.
- Investors: Only 16% of assessed companies show evidence of financially assessing different transition levers.
- Reporting teams: WBCSD’s findings favour clear status reporting and explanations of poor performance and corrective action.
- WBCSD members: The council will track reporting developments through engagement with its 250-plus members and reporting stakeholders.

articles.title: HKEX Opens Green Equity Designation With Annual Reviews
articles.summary:
HKEX has launched HKEX Green Equity, a voluntary designation for Hong Kong-listed companies with significant green business activities. Applications opened on 20 October 2026. Eligible companies will undergo independent assessment […]
The post HKEX Opens Green Equity Designation With Annual Reviews appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
HKEX Opens Green Equity Designation With Annual Reviews
- Application route: HKEX has opened voluntary applications from Hong Kong-listed companies with significant green business activities.
- Independent review: Recognised Reviewers will assess applicants under the HKEX Green Equity Framework.
- Ongoing checks: Successful companies may use the designation mark, subject to continuing compliance and annual reassessments.
HKEX has launched HKEX Green Equity, a voluntary designation for Hong Kong-listed companies with significant green business activities. Applications opened on 20 October 2026. Eligible companies will undergo independent assessment against the HKEX Green Equity Framework.
Successful applicants may use the designation mark while maintaining ongoing compliance and completing annual reassessments. Recognised Reviewers will evaluate how far each company’s activities contribute to the green economy. HKEX has published its approved reviewer list on a dedicated Green Equity webpage.
The programme aligns with similar globally recognised frameworks and promotes the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance in capital markets. It also aims to make qualifying green businesses more visible to investors globally. Investors can use the designation to identify companies that HKEX says make tangible contributions to the green economy.
HKEX invited current and prospective issuers with strong green-economy commitments to consider applying. The programme is voluntary, and companies must meet the framework requirements before receiving the designation. HKEX did not disclose application costs, assessment timelines or any initial applicants.
RELATED ARTICLE: Hong Kong Strengthens ESG Oversight as Family Offices Step Up
HKEX places the designation within its wider low-carbon transition ecosystem. That offering already spans climate disclosures and Core Climate products, including carbon credits and Green Electricity Certificates, known as GECs. “Investor demand for sustainable investment opportunities continues to grow, creating a greater need for credible and transparent ways to identify companies contributing to the green economy. Through a transparent framework and independent assessment process, HKEX Green Equity will help strengthen visibility for qualifying companies, support informed investment decisions and further reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a leading international sustainable finance hub. We strongly encourage our issuers and prospective issuers with a strong commitment to the green economy to consider applying for this important designation,” said Paul Chow, HKEX Group General Counsel and Group Chief Sustainability Officer.
Why It Matters
For HKEX, the programme adds a reviewed issuer designation with annual checks to its sustainability offering. Qualifying companies gain a mark and visibility among investors seeking businesses with tangible green-economy contributions. If issuers apply and retain approval, HKEX Green Equity could become a recurring investor filter and issuer service for green businesses.

articles.title: ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth
articles.summary:
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and […]
The post ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ECB Finds Euro Zone Oil Dependence Halved as AI and Fiscal Spending Support Growth
- Lower oil exposure: The euro zone economy is about half as reliant on oil as in the early 1990s, ECB economists estimate.
- Stronger fiscal support: Fiscal stimulus reached 0.5% of GDP, twice the level expected at the end of last year.
- Temporary growth drivers: ECB economists warn that AI investment, global demand and government spending may fade.
The euro zone economy has proved more resilient to this year’s energy shock than expected, according to European Central Bank (ECB) economists. Lower fossil fuel dependence, artificial intelligence investment and stronger government spending have helped sustain growth despite higher oil and gas prices.
Energy Dependence and Economic Resilience
ECB economists Oscar Arce, Gerrit Koester and Beatrice Pierluigi published the assessment in an ECB blog on Wednesday. They estimated that the euro area now relies on oil about half as much as in the early 1990s. This reduction has limited the economic impact of rising energy prices.
The Iran war disrupted energy markets, pushing oil and gas prices higher and renewing inflation concerns. However, the currency bloc has continued expanding, with business surveys showing that economic activity remains positive. Higher renewable and nuclear electricity generation has also weakened the connection between gas prices and electricity costs in several countries.
AI Investment and Fiscal Support
The ECB economists identified AI-related trade as an “important tailwind” for the euro area. Technology-related export orders and sectors linked to AI have outperformed, supporting economic activity during the energy shock.
Government spending has also exceeded earlier expectations. The fiscal impulse reached 0.5% of gross domestic product, twice the level projected at the end of last year. German government spending on defence and infrastructure accounted for much of the additional support.
However, the economists cautioned that several growth drivers could prove temporary. Global demand, fiscal stimulus and AI investment may weaken, particularly if geopolitical tensions intensify or energy markets face further disruption.
Monetary Policy Implications
The findings arrive as the ECB considers further interest rate increases to contain energy-driven inflation. A third rate increase this year is expected in December, following renewed inflation pressures and a global bond selloff.
The ECB assessment identifies reduced oil exposure as a structural source of resilience, alongside shorter-term support from investment and fiscal policy. However, its economists warn that fresh energy disruptions could leave the euro area vulnerable if those temporary sources of growth weaken.
RELATED ARTICLE: ECB Publishes Climate-Related Disclosures Showing Decarbonization Path
Who It Affects
- Euro zone businesses: Lower oil dependence and stronger electricity generation diversity have reduced exposure to energy price shocks in several countries.
- Technology exporters: AI-related investment and trade have supported stronger export orders and activity in AI-linked sectors.
- European policymakers: Energy-led inflation and the possibility of fading fiscal support complicate decisions on further interest rate increases.

articles.title: EU Methane Import Compliance Pushed to May 2031
articles.summary:
The European Parliament voted Thursday to approve a three-year delay to EU methane rules covering imported oil, gas and coal. Under Parliament’s proposal, affected importers would face the compliance deadline […]
The post EU Methane Import Compliance Pushed to May 2031 appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
EU Methane Import Compliance Pushed to May 2031
- Three-year delay: The European Parliament approved a longer postponement than the one-year delay expected several weeks earlier.
- Import contracts: Importers would have until May 31, 2031, to demonstrate compliance with equivalent EU methane measures.
- Next step: Parliament and EU governments must negotiate a final decision on the deadline.
The European Parliament voted Thursday to approve a three-year delay to EU methane rules covering imported oil, gas and coal. Under Parliament’s proposal, affected importers would face the compliance deadline on May 31, 2031.
The rules were originally due to take effect on January 1, 2027. They would have required foreign oil and gas suppliers serving the EU to monitor and report methane emissions. A one-year delay remained the expected outcome until several weeks before the vote. However, lobbying by France, the Czech Republic and Italy intensified support for a three-year postponement.
The United States had also pressed the EU over the requirements. In June, it warned that the methane law could disrupt fuel deliveries to Europe. ExxonMobil supported that position, while the United States was Europe’s largest liquefied natural gas supplier. Parliament’s statement did not specify penalties, enforcement mechanisms or scope thresholds.
Parliament’s proposal applies to supply contracts concluded or renewed from August 4, 2024. It covers crude oil, natural gas and coal subject to measures equivalent to EU requirements.
“Under Parliament’s proposal, importers of crude oil, natural gas and coal would have until May 31, 2031, to show that supply contracts concluded or renewed since August 4, 2024 cover only fuel subject to monitoring, reporting and verification measures equivalent to EU rules,” lawmakers said in a statement.
Methane is the second-largest contributor to climate change after carbon dioxide. Following Parliament’s vote, lawmakers must negotiate the final deadline with EU governments. The approved proposal therefore does not yet settle when the import requirements will apply.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Backs Carbon Market Changes to Curb Price Spikes
Who It Affects
- EU fuel importers: They would have until May 31, 2031, to show that relevant contracts cover fuel under equivalent measures.
- Foreign suppliers: Oil and gas suppliers serving the EU would monitor and report methane emissions under the delayed rules.
- United States suppliers: The United States warned that the law could disrupt fuel deliveries to Europe.
- EU governments: They must negotiate the final compliance deadline with European Parliament lawmakers.

articles.summary:
Asia may need to invest up to $1 trillion annually in energy over the next 15 years, according to McKinsey. The consultancy linked this requirement to efforts by countries to […]
The post McKinsey Sees Asia Energy Needs at $1 Trillion a Year Through 2040 appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
McKinsey Sees Asia Energy Needs at $1 Trillion a Year Through 2040
- Investment requirement: Asia may need up to $1 trillion in annual energy investment for the next 15 years.
- Demand forecast: McKinsey raised its 2040 estimate to 370 million terajoules, 15% above last year’s forecast.
- Renewables spending: Annual solar and wind investment could reach about $300 billion through 2040.
Asia may need to invest up to $1 trillion annually in energy over the next 15 years, according to McKinsey. The consultancy linked this requirement to efforts by countries to strengthen energy security after disrupted oil and gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz. It now forecasts regional energy demand of 370 million terajoules in 2040.
The revised demand estimate is 15% higher than McKinsey’s forecast from a year earlier. The consultancy expects Asia to generate about 70% of global net energy demand growth through 2040. New sources include data centres, alongside rising requirements from cooling and industrial activity.
McKinsey expects coal to remain in Asia’s energy mix longer than previously anticipated. Regional coal demand could remain broadly flat over the next decade. Falling consumption in China is expected to be offset by growth in India and Southeast Asia.
Gas demand is set to slow during the next five to 10 years. McKinsey said countries are prioritising coal and renewable energy for power generation. However, industrial demand could support a longer-term rebound in gas consumption.
Renewable energy deployment is expected to accelerate, particularly across India and Southeast Asia. McKinsey forecasts about $300 billion in annual solar and wind investment through 2040. The report summary did not disclose its methodology or underlying data period.
A stronger focus on energy security could support higher-cost upstream assets with government backing. McKinsey identified China, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and Turkmenistan as potential development markets. Meanwhile, biofuels could replace between $90 billion and $100 billion of fuel imports in 2040.
Who It Affects
- Asian governments: Energy security policies could support higher-cost upstream assets across five identified markets.
- Power producers: Near-term generation choices are expected to favour coal and renewables over gas.
- Renewable developers: India and Southeast Asia could anchor $300 billion in annual solar and wind investment.
- Fuel importers: Biofuels could reduce import dependence by replacing up to $100 billion of fuel imports in 2040.
